title: Choosing & Combining Models
html:
There is no single best algorithm (the “no free lunch” theorem) — but there are good defaults. Start simple, compare candidates with the same cross-validation, and combine models when it pays.

AlgorithmBoundary / shapeScaling neededInterpretabilityGood forWeak spots
Linear / logistic regressionLinearYes (when regularised)High (coefficients)Baselines, high-dimensional sparse data, probabilitiesNon-linear effects unless engineered
k-NNAny (local)YesMedium (show neighbours)Small, low-dimensional dataSlow predictions, high dimensions
Naive BayesLinear-ishNoMediumText, tiny data, speedCorrelated features, poor probabilities
SVM (RBF)Any (smooth)YesLowSmall/medium data, many featuresLarge n, needs tuning, no native probabilities
Decision treeAxis-aligned stepsNoHigh (rules)Explanations, rulesHigh variance
Random forestAxis-aligned, averagedNoMediumStrong default for tabular dataSize, extrapolation
Gradient boostingAxis-aligned, additiveNoMediumBest accuracy on most tabular problemsTuning, overfits without early stopping
Neural networksAnyYesLowImages, audio, text, very large dataData-hungry, tuning, compute

A practical order of attack

1
Baseline
DummyClassifier / DummyRegressor and any existing business rule.
2
Simple model
Regularised linear or logistic regression in a pipeline — fast, often surprisingly strong, and a sanity check for leakage.
3
Tree ensemble
Random forest, then gradient boosting (HistGradientBoosting / LightGBM / XGBoost) with early stopping.
4
Unstructured data
Pretrained deep models (fine-tuning or embeddings) — see Deep Learning and Generative AI.
5
Pick with constraints
Accuracy is one criterion; latency, memory, interpretability, calibration and maintenance matter too.

Compare candidates fairly

On this small, clean dataset the linear model is as good as anything — a reminder to always try the simple option. Differences inside one standard deviation are usually noise (see Hypothesis Tests & Significance for proper comparisons).

Voting and stacking

MethodHowNotes
Hard votingMajority of predicted labelsSimple; ignores confidence
Soft votingAverage predicted probabilitiesUsually better; needs reasonably calibrated models
StackingA meta-model learns how to combine base models' out-of-fold predictionsMost flexible; base models should be diverse
Watch out

Stacking must train the meta-model on out-of-fold predictions (StackingClassifier does this with its internal cv). Training it on predictions the base models made for their own training rows leaks — the meta-model learns to trust overfit models.

From ML to neural networks

Logistic regression is a one-neuron network: weighted sum → sigmoid → log-loss. A multi-layer perceptron stacks layers of such units with non-linear activations, so it can learn non-linear boundaries and its own features:

For anything beyond small experiments, neural networks are built in PyTorch or similar — backpropagation, optimisers, CNNs, RNNs and transformers are covered in Deep Learning.

How would you choose a model for a tabular classification problem?

Establish a dummy baseline, then a regularised logistic regression pipeline, then a tree ensemble (random forest, then gradient boosting with early stopping). Compare them with the same stratified CV folds on the metric that matters, check calibration and latency, and prefer the simpler model when the difference is within noise.

What is stacking and how do you avoid leakage in it?

A meta-model learns to combine the predictions of several base models. Its training inputs must be out-of-fold predictions (each row predicted by base models that didn't train on it); otherwise it learns from over-optimistic in-sample predictions.

What does the no-free-lunch theorem say?

Averaged over all possible problems, no learning algorithm beats any other. Every algorithm's success comes from assumptions that match the problem at hand — which is why we compare candidates empirically on our own data.
